guidance.title: Diabetic Foot
guidance.summary:
What is diabetes? 
 Diabetes is a disease in which your blood glucose, or blood sugar , levels are too high. Glucose comes from foods you eat. The cells of your body need glucose for energy. A hormone called insulin helps the glucose get into your cells. 
 With type 1 diabetes , your body doesn't make insulin. With type 2 diabetes , your body doesn't make or use insulin well. Without enough insulin, glucose can't get into your cells as quickly as usual. The glucose builds up in your blood and causes high blood sugar levels. 

 How does diabetes cause foot problems? 
 Foot problems are common in people with diabetes. They can happen over time when high blood sugar damages the nerves and blood vessels in the feet. The nerve damage, called diabetic neuropathy , can cause numbness, tingling, pain, or a loss of feeling in your feet. 
 If you can't feel pain, you may not know when you have a cut, blister , or ulcer (open sore) on your foot. A wound like that could get infected. The infection may not heal well because the damaged blood vessels can cause poor blood flow in your feet. 
 Having an infection and poor blood flow can lead to gangrene . That means the muscle, skin, and other tissues start to die. If you have gangrene or a foot ulcer that does not get better with treatment, you may need an amputation . This is a surgery to cut off your damaged toe, foot, or part of your leg. It may prevent a bad infection from spreading and could save your life. 
 But there's a lot you can do to prevent a foot wound from becoming a major health problem. 

 How can I protect my feet if I have diabetes?

guidance.title: Cellulitis and Cutaneous Abscess
guidance.summary:
1. **Missing necrotizing fasciitis by labeling it "just cellulitis."** Pain out of proportion to exam findings, crepitus, dusky skin, bullae, cutaneous anesthesia, rapid progression, and hemodynamic instability are red flags. A low LRINEC score does not exclude it. When in doubt, obtain surgical consultation and CT with contrast. Finger test (bedside fascial biopsy) at the advancing edge can confirm.

2. **Not performing POCUS to identify occult abscess.** Up to 50% of cases clinically diagnosed as cellulitis harbor a drainable abscess on ultrasound. A missed abscess will not resolve with antibiotics alone. Use POCUS liberally.

3. **Prescribing antibiotics for abscess without performing I&D.** Antibiotics alone have unacceptable failure rates for drainable abscess. I&D is the definitive treatment. Antibiotics are adjunctive.

4. **Using cephalexin monotherapy when MRSA abscess is likely.** Community-acquired MRSA prevalence in skin abscesses exceeds 50% in most US EDs. Purulent SSTIs and abscesses require MRSA coverage: TMP-SMX or doxycycline. Cephalexin does not cover MRSA.

5. **Failing to break up loculations during I&D.** An inadequately drained abscess with intact loculations will re-accumulate. Use a hemostat or finger to disrupt all septations within the abscess cavity.

6. **Not differentiating orbital from preseptal cellulitis.** Preseptal cellulitis (anterior to orbital septum) is managed with oral antibiotics. Orbital cellulitis (posterior to septum: proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, decreased visual acuity, pain with eye movement) requires CT, IV antibiotics, and ophthalmology/ENT consultation. Missed orbital cellulitis leads to vision loss, cavernous sinus thrombosis, or intracranial extension.

guidance.title: Cellulitis and Cutaneous Abscess
guidance.summary:
### Cellulitis (Non-Purulent SSTI)
- Spreading erythema, warmth, edema, tenderness without drainable collection
- Poorly defined borders, often unilateral
- Entry point: skin break, wound, tinea pedis, insect bite
- Most common pathogen: Group A Streptococcus (GAS), also Staphylococcus aureus
- Systemic signs: fever, tachycardia, lymphangitis, regional lymphadenopathy

### Cutaneous Abscess (Purulent SSTI)
- Fluctuant, tender, erythematous mass with overlying warmth
- Point tenderness, may have spontaneous drainage
- Most common pathogen: MRSA (prevalence 50-75% in community abscesses in the US)
- Common locations: axilla, groin, perirectal, buttock, face

### Severity Classification (IDSA)
| Class | Description | Management |
|---|---|---|
| Mild | No systemic signs, immunocompetent | Outpatient oral antibiotics or I&D alone |
| Moderate | Systemic signs (fever, tachycardia, WBC >12 or <4) OR immunocompromised OR failed outpatient therapy | IV antibiotics, observation or admit |
| Severe | Failed IV antibiotics, sepsis, deep space infection, necrotizing fasciitis | Surgical consultation, ICU |

### LRINEC Score (Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotizing Fasciitis)
| Parameter | Criteria | Points |
|---|---|---|
| CRP | ≥ 150 mg/L | 4 |
| WBC | 15-25 × 10⁹/L | 1 |
| WBC | > 25 × 10⁹/L | 2 |
| Hemoglobin | 11-13.5 g/dL | 1 |
| Hemoglobin | < 11 g/dL | 2 |
| Sodium | < 135 mEq/L | 2 |
| Creatinine | > 1.6 mg/dL | 2 |
| Glucose | > 180 mg/dL | 1 |

- Score ≥ 6: Intermediate/high risk for necrotizing fasciitis — surgical consultation
- Score ≥ 8: Strongly predictive — proceed to OR
- Sensitivity is imperfect (68-92%); clinical suspicion overrides a low score

 A callus with dried blood inside 
 A foot infection that becomes black and smells bad that could be gangrene

guidance.title: Cellulitis and Cutaneous Abscess
guidance.summary:
### Abscess: Incision and Drainage (I&D)
1. Prep with antiseptic (chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine)
2. Local anesthesia: lidocaine 1% with epinephrine (safe on all locations including digits — digital tourniquet epinephrine myth debunked). Field block around the abscess is more effective than direct injection into cavity.
3. Stab incision with #11 blade over point of maximal fluctuance, extending full length of cavity
4. Express purulent material; send culture
5. Break up all loculations with hemostat or finger (critical step)
6. Irrigate cavity with normal saline
7. Packing: traditional iodoform gauze packing OR loop drain (vessel loop through two stab incisions) — loop drain associated with less pain at follow-up and equivalent outcomes
8. Wound check in 48-72 hours for packing removal/replacement

### Antibiotics for Abscess (Post-I&D)
- Small abscess (< 2 cm) in immunocompetent: I&D alone may suffice (IDSA guidelines); however, recent RCTs (Talan 2016, Daum 2017) show adjunctive TMP-SMX improves cure rates
- **TMP-SMX DS (160/800 mg) 1-2 tabs PO BID x 7-10 days** — MRSA coverage
- **Doxycycline 100 mg PO BID x 7-10 days** — alternative MRSA coverage
- **Clindamycin 300-450 mg PO TID x 7-10 days** — alternative; check local resistance (inducible resistance up to 20-50%)

### Antibiotics for Cellulitis (Non-Purulent)
- **Mild (outpatient):**
  - Cephalexin 500 mg PO QID x 5-7 days (covers GAS, MSSA)
  - Dicloxacillin 500 mg PO QID x 5-7 days (alternative)
  - If MRSA risk: add TMP-SMX DS 1-2 tabs PO BID or doxycycline 100 mg PO BID
- **Moderate (IV):**
  - Cefazolin 1-2 g IV q8h
  - If MRSA risk: vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg IV q8-12h (target AUC/MIC 400-600) or daptomycin 4 mg/kg IV daily
- **Severe / Necrotizing fasciitis:**

guidance.title: Cellulitis and Cutaneous Abscess
guidance.summary:
### Discharge Criteria
- Mild cellulitis: immunocompetent, no systemic signs, reliable follow-up
- Abscess after I&D: pain controlled, no surrounding cellulitis/systemic signs, able to return for wound check in 48-72 hours
- Prescribe oral antibiotics, wound care instructions, clear return precautions

### Admission Criteria
- Systemic toxicity (fever, tachycardia, hypotension)
- Failed outpatient oral antibiotics (progression despite 48-72 hours of therapy)
- Immunocompromised (diabetes, HIV, transplant, chemotherapy)
- Extensive cellulitis requiring IV antibiotics
- Location requiring close monitoring (face, orbit, hand, perineum)
- Concern for necrotizing fasciitis or deep space infection — surgical consultation and admission
- Unable to tolerate oral medications

### Follow-Up
- Wound check 48-72 hours post-I&D
- Cellulitis re-evaluation at 48-72 hours to assess response (erythema should not extend beyond marked borders)
- Return immediately for: increasing pain, expanding erythema beyond marks, fever, systemic symptoms, crepitus, skin color change to dusky/purple

guidance.title: Diabetic Nerve Problems
guidance.summary:
If you have diabetes , your blood glucose, or blood sugar , levels are too high. Over time, this can damage the covering on your nerves or the blood vessels that bring oxygen to your nerves. Damaged nerves may stop sending messages, or may send messages slowly or at the wrong times. 

 This damage is called diabetic neuropathy. Over half of people with diabetes get it. Symptoms may include: 
 Numbness in your hands, legs, or feet 
 Shooting pains, burning, or tingling 
 Nausea, vomiting, constipation, or diarrhea 
 Problems with sexual function 
 Urinary problems 
 Dizziness when you change positions quickly 
 

 Your doctor will diagnose diabetic neuropathy with a physical exam and nerve tests. Controlling your blood sugar can help prevent nerve problems, or keep them from getting worse. Treatment may include pain relief and other medicines. 

 NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases

guidance.title: Hepatic Abscess
guidance.summary:
1. **Missing Klebsiella pneumoniae invasive syndrome.** K. pneumoniae liver abscess (especially K1/K2 serotype) metastasizes to eyes (endophthalmitis → blindness) and CNS. Screen diabetic patients with KPLA with ophthalmology exam and neurologic assessment.

2. **Aspirating an echinococcal cyst mistaken for abscess.** Unprotected aspiration of hydatid cyst causes anaphylaxis and peritoneal seeding. If there is any concern for echinococcus (endemic exposure, calcified wall, daughter cysts), obtain Echinococcus serology BEFORE aspiration.

3. **Insufficient antibiotic duration.** Hepatic abscesses require prolonged therapy (4-6 weeks total). Premature discontinuation leads to recurrence. Follow CRP and imaging to guide duration.

4. **Failing to evaluate for underlying GI malignancy.** Cryptogenic pyogenic liver abscess in patients > 50 is associated with occult colorectal cancer. Colonoscopy after acute phase is mandatory.

5. **Not adding a luminal agent after treating amebic abscess.** Metronidazole alone does not eradicate intestinal colonization. Paromomycin is required to prevent relapse. Omission is the most common error in amebic abscess management.

6. **Treating amebic abscess with drainage first.** Unlike pyogenic abscesses, most amebic abscesses respond to metronidazole alone. Drainage is reserved for large (> 10 cm), left-lobe (pericardial rupture risk), or refractory abscesses.

guidance.title: Sepsis and Septic Shock
guidance.summary:
1. **Delaying antibiotics to obtain cultures.** Draw cultures, then immediately administer antibiotics. Never wait for culture results, LP results, or imaging before giving antibiotics in septic shock.

2. **Using qSOFA as a diagnostic tool rather than a screening tool.** A qSOFA < 2 does NOT exclude sepsis. It was designed for bedside prognostication, not diagnosis. Use clinical judgment and SOFA scoring.

3. **Attributing altered mental status to "baseline" in elderly patients.** Acute confusion is an organ dysfunction marker. Assume sepsis until proven otherwise in elderly patients with altered mentation and any infection risk.

4. **Over-resuscitating with crystalloid without reassessing.** Fluid overload worsens outcomes, especially in ARDS. Reassess with POCUS after every 500-1000 mL. Start vasopressors early if MAP remains < 65 despite 1-2 L.

5. **Failing to identify and control the source.** Antibiotics alone will not resolve undrained abscesses, obstructed viscera, or necrotizing infections. Imaging and surgical consultation are part of first-hour management when source is uncertain.

6. **Not considering occult sources in patients with negative initial workup.** Endocarditis, epidural abscess, prosthetic joint infection, and C. difficile colitis may not be apparent on initial evaluation. Broaden the search when cultures are negative and the patient is not improving.

7. **Underdosing vancomycin.** Use actual body weight for the loading dose (25-30 mg/kg). A 100 kg patient needs 2.5-3 g, not the traditional 1 g.

chunk.text:
What is diabetes? 
 Diabetes is a disease in which your blood glucose, or blood sugar , levels are too high. Glucose comes from foods you eat. The cells of your body need glucose for energy. A hormone called insulin helps the glucose get into your cells. 
 With type 1 diabetes , your body doesn't make insulin. With type 2 diabetes , your body doesn't make or use insulin well. Without enough insulin, glucose can't get into your cells as quickly as usual. The glucose builds up in your blood and causes high blood sugar levels. 

 How does diabetes cause foot problems? 
 Foot problems are common in people with diabetes. They can happen over time when high blood sugar damages the nerves and blood vessels in the feet. The nerve damage, called diabetic neuropathy , can cause numbness, tingling, pain, or a loss of feeling in your feet. 
 If you can't feel pain, you may not know when you have a cut, blister , or ulcer (open sore) on your foot. A wound like that could get infected. The infection may not heal well because the damaged blood vessels can cause poor blood flow in your feet. 
 Having an infection and poor blood flow can lead to gangrene . That means the muscle, skin, and other tissues start to die. If you have gangrene or a foot ulcer that does not get better with treatment, you may need an amputation . This is a surgery to cut off your damaged toe, foot, or part of your leg. It may prevent a bad infection from spreading and could save your life. 
 But there's a lot you can do to prevent a foot wound from becoming a major health problem. 

 How can I protect my feet if I have diabetes?

If you have diabetes , your blood glucose, or blood sugar , levels are too high. Over time, this can damage the covering on your nerves or the blood vessels that bring oxygen to your nerves. Damaged nerves may stop sending messages, or may send messages slowly or at the wrong times. 

 This damage is called diabetic neuropathy. Over half of people with diabetes get it. Symptoms may include: 
 Numbness in your hands, legs, or feet 
 Shooting pains, burning, or tingling 
 Nausea, vomiting, constipation, or diarrhea 
 Problems with sexual function 
 Urinary problems 
 Dizziness when you change positions quickly 
 

 Your doctor will diagnose diabetic neuropathy with a physical exam and nerve tests. Controlling your blood sugar can help prevent nerve problems, or keep them from getting worse. Treatment may include pain relief and other medicines.

1. **Missing necrotizing fasciitis by labeling it "just cellulitis."** Pain out of proportion to exam findings, crepitus, dusky skin, bullae, cutaneous anesthesia, rapid progression, and hemodynamic instability are red flags. A low LRINEC score does not exclude it. When in doubt, obtain surgical consultation and CT with contrast. Finger test (bedside fascial biopsy) at the advancing edge can confirm.

2. **Not performing POCUS to identify occult abscess.** Up to 50% of cases clinically diagnosed as cellulitis harbor a drainable abscess on ultrasound. A missed abscess will not resolve with antibiotics alone. Use POCUS liberally.

3. **Prescribing antibiotics for abscess without performing I&D.** Antibiotics alone have unacceptable failure rates for drainable abscess. I&D is the definitive treatment. Antibiotics are adjunctive.

4. **Using cephalexin monotherapy when MRSA abscess is likely.** Community-acquired MRSA prevalence in skin abscesses exceeds 50% in most US EDs. Purulent SSTIs and abscesses require MRSA coverage: TMP-SMX or doxycycline. Cephalexin does not cover MRSA.

5. **Failing to break up loculations during I&D.** An inadequately drained abscess with intact loculations will re-accumulate. Use a hemostat or finger to disrupt all septations within the abscess cavity.

### Abscess: Incision and Drainage (I&D)
1. Prep with antiseptic (chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine)
2. Local anesthesia: lidocaine 1% with epinephrine (safe on all locations including digits — digital tourniquet epinephrine myth debunked). Field block around the abscess is more effective than direct injection into cavity.
3. Stab incision with #11 blade over point of maximal fluctuance, extending full length of cavity
4. Express purulent material; send culture
5. Break up all loculations with hemostat or finger (critical step)
6. Irrigate cavity with normal saline
7. Packing: traditional iodoform gauze packing OR loop drain (vessel loop through two stab incisions) — loop drain associated with less pain at follow-up and equivalent outcomes

1. **Missing Klebsiella pneumoniae invasive syndrome.** K. pneumoniae liver abscess (especially K1/K2 serotype) metastasizes to eyes (endophthalmitis → blindness) and CNS. Screen diabetic patients with KPLA with ophthalmology exam and neurologic assessment.

2. **Aspirating an echinococcal cyst mistaken for abscess.** Unprotected aspiration of hydatid cyst causes anaphylaxis and peritoneal seeding. If there is any concern for echinococcus (endemic exposure, calcified wall, daughter cysts), obtain Echinococcus serology BEFORE aspiration.

3. **Insufficient antibiotic duration.** Hepatic abscesses require prolonged therapy (4-6 weeks total). Premature discontinuation leads to recurrence. Follow CRP and imaging to guide duration.

4. **Failing to evaluate for underlying GI malignancy.** Cryptogenic pyogenic liver abscess in patients > 50 is associated with occult colorectal cancer. Colonoscopy after acute phase is mandatory.

5. **Not adding a luminal agent after treating amebic abscess.** Metronidazole alone does not eradicate intestinal colonization. Paromomycin is required to prevent relapse. Omission is the most common error in amebic abscess management.

6. **Treating amebic abscess with drainage first.** Unlike pyogenic abscesses, most amebic abscesses respond to metronidazole alone. Drainage is reserved for large (> 10 cm), left-lobe (pericardial rupture risk), or refractory abscesses.

1. **Not covering anaerobes empirically.** Primary lung abscesses are predominantly caused by anaerobic bacteria from aspiration. Standard CAP antibiotics (azithromycin + ceftriaxone) do not adequately cover anaerobes. Use ampicillin-sulbactam or clindamycin-based regimens.

2. **Stopping antibiotics too early.** Lung abscesses require prolonged therapy (4-6 weeks minimum). Premature discontinuation leads to relapse and complications. Imaging resolution lags behind clinical improvement — do not stop based on the patient feeling better alone.

3. **Missing cavitary lung cancer disguised as abscess.** Patients > 50 years, smokers, or those who fail to respond to appropriate antibiotics should undergo bronchoscopy or CT-guided biopsy. Squamous cell carcinoma commonly presents as a cavitary lesion.

4. **Failing to position the patient for postural drainage.** Positioning the patient with the abscess on the dependent side promotes gravitational drainage through the airways. This is an important adjunct to antibiotic therapy and is often overlooked.

5. **Inadequate evaluation for empyema.** Lung abscess frequently coexists with empyema or can rupture into the pleural space. CT chest should assess for concurrent pleural infection. Empyema requires tube thoracostomy in addition to antibiotics.

chunk.text:
### Cellulitis (Non-Purulent SSTI)
- Spreading erythema, warmth, edema, tenderness without drainable collection
- Poorly defined borders, often unilateral
- Entry point: skin break, wound, tinea pedis, insect bite
- Most common pathogen: Group A Streptococcus (GAS), also Staphylococcus aureus
- Systemic signs: fever, tachycardia, lymphangitis, regional lymphadenopathy

### Cutaneous Abscess (Purulent SSTI)
- Fluctuant, tender, erythematous mass with overlying warmth
- Point tenderness, may have spontaneous drainage
- Most common pathogen: MRSA (prevalence 50-75% in community abscesses in the US)
- Common locations: axilla, groin, perirectal, buttock, face

### Severity Classification (IDSA)
| Class | Description | Management |
|---|---|---|
| Mild | No systemic signs, immunocompetent | Outpatient oral antibiotics or I&D alone |
| Moderate | Systemic signs (fever, tachycardia, WBC >12 or <4) OR immunocompromised OR failed outpatient therapy | IV antibiotics, observation or admit |
| Severe | Failed IV antibiotics, sepsis, deep space infection, necrotizing fasciitis | Surgical consultation, ICU |

### LRINEC Score (Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotizing Fasciitis)
| Parameter | Criteria | Points |
|---|---|---|
| CRP | ≥ 150 mg/L | 4 |
| WBC | 15-25 × 10⁹/L | 1 |
| WBC | > 25 × 10⁹/L | 2 |
| Hemoglobin | 11-13.5 g/dL | 1 |
| Hemoglobin | < 11 g/dL | 2 |
| Sodium | < 135 mEq/L | 2 |
| Creatinine | > 1.6 mg/dL | 2 |
| Glucose | > 180 mg/dL | 1 |

- Score ≥ 6: Intermediate/high risk for necrotizing fasciitis — surgical consultation
- Score ≥ 8: Strongly predictive — proceed to OR
- Sensitivity is imperfect (68-92%); clinical suspicion overrides a low score

### Discharge Criteria
- Mild cellulitis: immunocompetent, no systemic signs, reliable follow-up
- Abscess after I&D: pain controlled, no surrounding cellulitis/systemic signs, able to return for wound check in 48-72 hours
- Prescribe oral antibiotics, wound care instructions, clear return precautions

### Admission Criteria
- Systemic toxicity (fever, tachycardia, hypotension)
- Failed outpatient oral antibiotics (progression despite 48-72 hours of therapy)
- Immunocompromised (diabetes, HIV, transplant, chemotherapy)
- Extensive cellulitis requiring IV antibiotics
- Location requiring close monitoring (face, orbit, hand, perineum)
- Concern for necrotizing fasciitis or deep space infection — surgical consultation and admission
- Unable to tolerate oral medications

### Follow-Up
- Wound check 48-72 hours post-I&D
- Cellulitis re-evaluation at 48-72 hours to assess response (erythema should not extend beyond marked borders)
- Return immediately for: increasing pain, expanding erythema beyond marks, fever, systemic symptoms, crepitus, skin color change to dusky/purple

### Sepsis-3 Definitions

**Sepsis:** Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. Operationalized as suspected infection + acute increase in SOFA score >= 2.

**Septic shock:** Sepsis with persistent hypotension requiring vasopressors to maintain MAP >= 65 mmHg AND serum lactate > 2 mmol/L despite adequate volume resuscitation.

### qSOFA (Quick SOFA) - Bedside Screening
- Respiratory rate >= 22/min
- Altered mentation (GCS < 15)
- Systolic BP <= 100 mmHg
- Score >= 2 associated with poor outcomes; prompts further assessment. Not a diagnostic criterion.

### SOFA Score Components (baseline = 0 for all unless known prior dysfunction)
- PaO2/FiO2 ratio
- Platelet count
- Bilirubin
- Cardiovascular (MAP and vasopressor requirements)
- GCS
- Creatinine or urine output

### Clinical Clues by Source
| Source | Findings |
|---|---|
| Pulmonary | Cough, hypoxia, crackles, consolidation on CXR |
| Urinary | Dysuria, flank pain, pyuria, CVA tenderness |
| Abdominal | Tenderness, rigidity, distension, peritoneal signs |
| Skin/soft tissue | Cellulitis, crepitus, purulent drainage, necrotizing fasciitis |
| CNS | Meningismus, photophobia, altered mental status |
| Line-related | Erythema/purulence at catheter site, tunneled line without other source |

### High-Risk Populations
- Immunosuppressed (transplant, chemotherapy, HIV with CD4 < 200, chronic steroids)
- Extremes of age (neonates, elderly)
- Indwelling devices (central lines, urinary catheters, prosthetic joints)
- Asplenic patients (encapsulated organisms: pneumococcus, meningococcus, H. influenzae)
- IV drug users (endocarditis, epidural abscess)

1. **Treating as simple cellulitis.** Pain out of proportion to skin findings, systemic toxicity, and failure to improve on antibiotics are red flags. If any hard sign is present, proceed directly to operative exploration.

2. **Relying on a low LRINEC score to rule out necrotizing fasciitis.** The LRINEC score has limited sensitivity (~60-80%). Clinical suspicion must override scoring. When in doubt, take the patient to the OR.

3. **Delaying surgery for imaging.** CT and MRI can support the diagnosis but are neither 100% sensitive nor specific. If clinical suspicion is high, operative exploration is both diagnostic and therapeutic. Every hour of surgical delay increases mortality.

4. **Performing a single debridement and declaring the patient treated.** Necrotizing fasciitis requires serial debridements. The infection often extends beyond the initial operative field. Return to OR in 24-48h is standard.

5. **Omitting clindamycin.** Clindamycin inhibits toxin production at the ribosomal level. In GAS and Staphylococcal infections, toxin-mediated tissue destruction continues even after bactericidal antibiotics kill the organism. Clindamycin addresses this mechanism.

6. **Missing Fournier gangrene.** Perineal necrotizing fasciitis (Fournier gangrene) in diabetics or immunocompromised patients may present with subtle perineal pain and scrotal swelling. Digital rectal exam and perineal inspection are essential in patients with perineal/genital complaints and sepsis.
